entries.name: Gift wrapping algorithm
entries.description: An algorithm for constructing the smallest shape that wraps a collection of points.

entries.name: Backtracking
entries.description: When you explore a search space and you reach a dead end, you follow your tracks back to the last crossroad and try the other way.

entries.name: Brute force
entries.description: Violence is actually almost always a solution, but not a very clever one.

entries.name: Greedy algorithm
entries.description: An algorithm that finds a solution by always picking the currently best-looking option without thinking too much about past and future decisions.

entries.name: Hill climbing
entries.description: Starting somewhere in the hilly "landscape" of solutions, you go in the direction of steepest ascent until reaching the top of a hill. You might miss higher hills, though.

entries.name: Israeli Queue
entries.description: A type of priority queue and a reference to the infamously unorganized queues in Israel. Here items can cut in line when they have already waiting friends.

entries.name: Sieve of Eratosthenes
entries.description: An ancient algorithm for finding all prime numbers up to a given limit. Non-primes are methodically sifted out, like unwanted material filtered through a sieve.

entries.name: Simulated annealing
entries.description: An optimization algorithm inspired by the metallurgical process of annealing, where slowly cooling a heated material allows it to settle into a low-energy, globally optimal state.

entries.name: Stack
entries.description: Like with a stack of pancakes, you can only add and remove items from the top of this data structure.

entries.name: Tree
entries.description: A hierarchically organized data structure. From the root item, the other items branch out into nodes and leaves. A collection of trees is often called a forest.

entries.name: Queue
entries.description: In this data structure, items are always added at the end and removed at the front as if the items were waiting in line.

entries.name: Adapter
entries.description: Allows classes with incompatible interfaces to work together by wrapping its own interface around that of an already existing class.

entries.name: Decorator
entries.description: Adds new responsibilities to an object by wrapping it in a layer of additional behavior, just as you can decorate a room without changing its walls.

entries.name: Facade
entries.description: Analogous to a facade in architecture, a facade is an object that serves as a front-facing interface masking more complex underlying structure.

entries.name: God object
entries.description: An anti-pattern where a single object knows too much or does too much. Like a god, it is omniscient and omnipotent.

entries.name: Promise
entries.description: A representation of a result that is available in the future, unless there are errors. Like in reality, promises are broken sometimes.

entries.name: Shotgun surgery
entries.description: A programming antipattern where, in a single change, you wildly add code everywhere in your codebase.

entries.name: Spaghetti Code
entries.description: A program with a tangled and hard-to-follow stucture.

entries.name: fold
entries.description: Like a blanket being folded up, this function iterates a collection and in each step combines the current item with everything that has already been folded.

entries.name: munch
entries.description: Parser function that greedily consumes an input stream until it's satisfied.

entries.name: trampoline
entries.description: Continuously runs functions that themselves return functions. Like a child on a trampoline that returns and bounces back up.

entries.name: zip
entries.description: Merges two lists into one list of pairs like the interlocking teeth of a zipper.

entries.name: Backdoor
entries.description: A method of bypassing normal authentication in a computer system.

entries.name: Canary
entries.description: A secret value placed on the stack to detect buffer overflow attacks. If it has been altered, danger is near — just like a canary in a coal mine that warns miners of toxic gas.

entries.name: Computer virus
entries.description: A computer program that self-replicates by infecting other computer programs, similar to the behavior of biological viruses.

entries.name: Cyber hygiene
entries.description: Steps and practices that users should take to maintain system health and improve online security.

entries.name: Honeypot
entries.description: Part of a system meant to look like an attractive target but actually helps detect and deflect attackers.

entries.name: Phishing
entries.description: Refers to the use of lures to "fish" for sensitive information.

entries.name: Phoning home
entries.description: When a system (e.g. stolen computer) secretly reports back to a third party other than the current possessor. The name is a reference to the movie E.T.

entries.name: Sandbox
entries.description: A safe and isolated environment to test unverified programs that may contain malicious code.

entries.name: Trojan horse
entries.description: Malware which misleads users of its true intent. The term is derived from the Ancient Greek story of the deceptive Trojan Horse.

entries.name: Attention
entries.description: A mechanism allowing models to selectively focus on the most relevant parts of their input, just as humans direct their attention to what matters most.

entries.name: Confusion matrix
entries.description: A tabular summary of a classifier's "confusion", i.e., how often it thought to make correct predictions when it actually didn't.

entries.name: Decision boundary
entries.description: A boundary dividing the space of possible data points. Here you decide, everything on this side is SPAM, everything on that side is not.

entries.name: Dropout
entries.description: Randomly disabling neurons during training to prevent overfitting. Like a sports team that improves by practicing with random members absent.

entries.name: Gradient descent
entries.description: Minimizing a cost function by iteratively computing the gradient and moving in the direction of steepest descent.

entries.name: Hallucination
entries.description: A confident response by an AI that does not seem to be justified by its training data.

entries.name: Training
entries.description: The process of showing the machine a bunch of examples, until it learns what we want from it.

entries.name: Choreographic programming
entries.description: A programming paradigm where programs are compositions of interactions among multiple concurrent participants.
section: Programming Languages and Programming Language Theory

entries.name: Clojure
entries.description: A functional language making extensive use of closures but with a j because it's running on the Java virtual machine.
section: Programming Languages and Programming Language Theory

entries.name: C++
entries.description: Although C was certainly a bad name, C++ was quite clever. The iconic increment operator ++ indicates that C++ is the successor.
section: Programming Languages and Programming Language Theory

entries.name: Garbage Collector
entries.description: Part of a program that attempts to find and reclaim garbage pieces of memory not used anymore.
section: Programming Languages and Programming Language Theory

entries.name: Lazy evaluation
entries.description: An evaluation strategy which suspends evaluation until it's absolutely necessary and then never does it again.
section: Programming Languages and Programming Language Theory

entries.name: Syntactic sugar
entries.description: Syntax that makes the language "sweeter" for human use. Usually a shorthand for common operations that can also be expressed in a more verbose form.
section: Programming Languages and Programming Language Theory

entries.name: Bento layout
entries.description: A grid-based layout resembling the compartmentation of bento boxes.

entries.name: Breadcrumb
entries.description: Navigational aid allowing users to keep track of their location within programs, documents, or websites. The term is a reference to the fairy tale Hansel and Gretel.

entries.name: Carousel
entries.description: A kind of animated slideshow looping back on itself.

entries.name: Clipboard
entries.description: Where you temporarily put files you are working with (i.e. the copy & paste buffer).

entries.name: Desktop
entries.description: The metaphorical top of the user's desk, upon which objects such as documents and folders of documents can be placed.

entries.name: Hamburger button
entries.description: A button to toggle a menu. The associated icon resembles a hamburger.

entries.name: Optimistic UI
entries.description: User interfaces that assume expensive operations will complete successfully, thereby improving the perceived performance.

entries.name: Scrolling
entries.description: Screen content is often less like a book with discrete pages and more like a continuous roll of parchment, i.e., a scroll.

entries.name: Toast notification
entries.description: A small message that briefly pops up at the edge of the screen and then disappears on its own, just like toast from a toaster.

entries.name: Busy Beaver
entries.description: Turing machines that produce numbers so insanely large, no other algorithm can keep up with them.

entries.name: Clique problem
entries.description: The problem of finding groups of mutual friends in a network of people with friendship relations. Or more generally, finding complete subgraphs.

entries.name: Game of Life
entries.description: A game world that showcases how astonishing complexity can arise from very simple ingredients.

entries.name: Oracle
entries.description: A black box that magically gives answers even to undecidable questions like the halting problem.

entries.name: Pumping lemma
entries.description: The fact that in some formal languages any sufficiently long string can be pumped with repetitions of its substring and the result stays in the same formal language.

entries.name: bubblewrap
entries.description: Sandboxing tool forming a protective layer for your system.

entries.name: caffeinate
entries.description: Terminal app to keep MacOS from "sleeping".

entries.name: clooney
entries.description: A JavaScript library implementing the actor model for concurrent computation. The term is a reference to George Clooney, who is also an actor.

entries.name: CockroachDB
entries.description: Database application, that is marketed as being so fault-tolerant and resilient as a cockroach.

entries.name: corrosion
entries.description: The process that turns metal into rust (literally), but also a tool that "turns" C++ into Rust.

entries.name: git bayesect
entries.description: Like git bisect but can cope with flaky tests using Baysian inferance.

entries.name: go-brrr
entries.description: Pure Go implementation of the brotli compression algorithm . Also a reference to the go brrr meme.

entries.name: horcrux
entries.description: Splits a file into encrypted fragments that only together can be decrypted again. In the Harry Potter universe, Horcruxes are fragments of a person's soul. To kill the person, all fragments must be destroyed.

entries.name: Puppeteer
entries.description: A browser automation library. If the browser is the puppet, this is the puppeteer.

entries.name: Safari
entries.description: Web browser developed by Apple.

entries.name: tldr
entries.description: Simplified man pages with practical examples.

entries.name: Uglify
entries.description: A JavaScript minifier. Removes everything that makes the code readable and pretty to make it smaller.

entries.name: uppy
entries.description: A dog-themed uploader component. The name is a blend of upload and puppy. It even comes with a crash recovery plugin called Golden Retriever.

entries.name: Webpack
entries.description: A bundler for JavaScript and other web assets with a short and descriptive name that also somewhat rhymes.

entries.name: yarn
entries.description: NodeJS dependency manager.

entries.name: a11y, i18n, k8s, ...
entries.description: Abbreviating long words by keeping the first and last letter and writing the number of omitted letters in between.

entries.name: ACID vs. BASE
entries.description: Acronyms describing competing database ideologies (aka. SQL vs. NoSQL). Note that acid and base are also opposites in chemistry.

entries.name: Bottleneck
entries.description: A central part of a network/application that significantly limits throughput/performance and should ideally be eliminated.

entries.name: Brick
entries.description: When your device is so corrupted, it virtually turns into a brick.

entries.name: camelCase, snake_case, kebab-case
entries.description: Different case styles where the name illustrates its appearance.

entries.name: Code golf
entries.description: Writing a program in as few characters as possible. Just like how Golf players try to win in the fewest club strokes.

entries.name: Cookie licking
entries.description: E.g., claiming a GitHub issue, then not working on it.

entries.name: Easter egg
entries.description: A hidden feature, especially in video games, in reference to the Easter egg hunt.

entries.name: Firmware
entries.description: The ware between software and hardware.

entries.name: Floating point number
entries.description: This representation can encode numbers at very different magnitudes with a limited amount of digits by letting the radix point float instead of being fixed in place.

entries.name: Framework
entries.description: In software architecture (like in actual architecture), frameworks provide a basic structure to build upon, guiding and constraining further development.

entries.name: Glue Code
entries.description: Jenga and LEGO bricks don't share the same interface, but you can always glue them together.

entries.name: Great Firewall of China
entries.description: Chinas controversial internet censorship system and a reference to the Great Wall of China.

entries.name: Heartbeat
entries.description: A periodic signal a system sends to confirm it is still alive and functioning, just like a pulse.

entries.name: Heisenbug
entries.description: A bug that seems to disappear or change when one tries to study it. It's a pun on Werner Heisenberg, who discovered that the act of observing quantum systems inevitably alters their state.

entries.name: Hydra
entries.description: A bug that, when an attempt to fix it is made, introduces multiple new bugs. It's a bug that cannot be fixed.

entries.name: Magic
entries.description: A magic program/piece of code is doing its job, but nobody knows how. Like in reality, magic doesn't actually exist. Once you understand it, it's not magic anymore.

entries.name: Process starvation
entries.description: A problem where a process is perpetually denied resources to do its work.

entries.name: Technical debt
entries.description: The implied future cost of shortcuts taken today, which accumulates like financial debt and must eventually be paid back — often with interest.

entries.name: Time travel debugging
entries.description: Stepping back in time through source code to understand execution and sometimes even to change history.

entries.name: Tree shaking
entries.description: Shake the dependency tree until all the dead parts are falling off and you end up with a nice lean tree.

entries.name: Unfair enumeration
entries.description: A program that outputs all even numbers and then all odd numbers generates an unfair enumeration of the natural numbers because some numbers are never reached.

entries.name: Yoda condition
entries.description: When you write if ("red" === color) { instead of if (color === "red") { because it reads as, “if red equals the color”, similar to the way the Star Wars character Yoda speaks.
